title: Project scoping and architecture design
notes: Scope an agent to one job done well, and write down what it will not do and who handles that instead.
Decide how you will measure success before you build: a pass rate target, zero policy breaks and zero invented facts.
Draw the architecture first: the customer, the agent loop, tools, data, memory, a trace and a path to a person.

slides.title: Project scoping and architecture design
slides.sub: Decide Scout's one job, its limits and its shape before you write code
sentences: You've built every part of an agent: a model, tools, memory and a loop.
In this module you put them together into one working project, Scout, Orbit's support agent.
Before writing any code, you make two decisions that save days later.
What exactly is Scout's job, and what does it look like on paper?

slides.title: Two ways to start a project

left.label: Scout does everything
points: No clear way to tell if it works

right.label: One job, done well
points: Six tools, each with one purpose
A test set that says if it works

sentences: When Maya first heard about Scout, she had a long wish list.
Answer order questions, write marketing emails, update the stock sheet, recommend tents, and more.
Every extra job means more tools, and more tools mean more chances to pick the wrong one.
Worse, with ten jobs there is no single way to say whether Scout works.
So we scope it to one job: answering order, return and exchange questions.
That job is narrow enough to test, and it covers most of Leo's tickets.
It's the difference between shipping in three weeks and never shipping at all.

slides.title: Inside the job, and outside it

cells: Looks it up and tracks it

note.text: Writing down what Scout will not do is part of the design.

sentences: Scoping means being exact, so let's sort some real requests from Leo's queue.
Questions like where is my order are Scout's core job: it looks the order up and tracks the parcel.
Returns and exchanges are in too, because Scout can check the order, the policy and the stock.
Refunds over two hundred dollars are half in: Scout starts them, and a person approves them.
Product advice needs real gear expertise, so Scout hands that chat to a person.
Marketing emails are not Scout's job at all, so it never tries.
Writing down what Scout will not do matters just as much as what it will do.

slides.title: How we'll know Scout works
sentences: Next, decide how you will know Scout works, before you build it.
First, right answers: on a set of real test questions, Scout should pass 90 percent or more.
Second, policy kept: no refund over two hundred dollars without a person, and no promise the policy doesn't make.
Third, nothing invented: when a tool fails or data is missing, Scout says so instead of guessing.
The last two targets are zero, because one broken promise costs more than ten clumsy replies.

slides.title: Scout's architecture on one page

note.text: Draw this before you code. Every box becomes a file or a function.

sentences: Now draw the shape of the whole system on one page.
In the middle sits Scout's loop, and a customer talks to it.
Scout reaches the outside world only through its six tools.
The tools read Orbit's data: the orders, the stock levels and the policy file.
Memory keeps the recent conversation, plus pinned facts like the order number.
A hand-off path passes the chat to a person when Scout should stop.
And a trace records every step, so you can see what happened when something goes wrong.
Each box on this page becomes a file or a function in your project.

slides.title: One question, through the architecture

note.text: Every result goes back to the loop. Scout replies only once it has the facts.

sentences: Let's follow one real question through that drawing.
Ana asks where her tent is, and gives her order number.
Scout's loop decides it needs facts, so it asks for a tool.
First the get order tool, then the track parcel tool, using the tracking number it just found.
Those tools read Orbit's order file and the carrier's tracking service.
With the facts in hand, Scout replies: shipped, and arriving Thursday.
If any tool fails, the loop sees the error, and Scout says so instead of guessing.

slides.title: Scout at the edge of its job

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: My Storm jacket is too big. Can I swap it for a medium?

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Good news, Owen: the medium is in stock, and exchanging for a different size is free.

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: Great. Also, which rope should I buy for ice climbing?

messages.label: hand_off
messages.text: Owen, ORB-10588: exchange L for M is possible. Wants rope advice for ice climbing.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: That's one for our gear experts. I've passed it to the team with a summary, so you won't have to repeat yourself.

aside.label: Hand-off, not a guess
aside.text: Outside its job, Scout passes the chat on with a summary instead of inventing advice.

sentences: Here is the scope working in a real chat.
Owen asks to swap his jacket for a smaller size.
That's inside the job, so Scout checks the stock and answers.
Then Owen asks which rope to buy for ice climbing.
Gear advice is outside Scout's job, so it calls the hand off tool with a short summary.
Scout tells Owen a person will pick it up, and he won't have to explain it again.
A clean hand-off is part of the design, not a failure.

slides.title: Recap

points.text: Scope to one job: order, return and exchange questions.
Write down what Scout will not do, and who handles it instead.
Set measures first: a pass rate, zero policy breaks, zero guesses.
Draw the architecture: loop, tools, data, memory, hand-off, trace.

sentences: Let's recap.
Scout has one job, order, return and exchange questions, done well.
You wrote down what it will not do, and who handles those requests instead.
You set measures before building: a pass rate target, and zero policy breaks or invented facts.
And you drew the architecture, so every box already has a place in the code.
Next, you build it, one small piece at a time.

midQuiz.q: Maya asks for Scout to also update Sam's stock sheet. What does good scoping say?
options: Add it now: one more tool is cheap
Keep it out for now: it's a different job with its own risks and tests
Add it quietly through the system prompt so the tests don't change
midQuiz.explain: Every extra job adds tools to choose between and new ways to fail. Scout ships sooner and safer doing one job well; the stock sheet can be its own project.
midQuiz.hint: Think about what each new job adds to the test set.

midQuiz.q: Which of these is a success measure you can actually check?
options: Customers will love talking to Scout
At least 90 percent of 60 real test questions pass
midQuiz.explain: A measure you can check is specific: a set of test questions, a check and a target number. The others are hopes.
midQuiz.hint: Which one gives you a number you could compare next week?

endQuiz.q: In Scout's architecture, how does the agent loop reach Orbit's order data?
options: Only through its tools, like get_order
The whole order file is pasted into the system prompt
The model remembers the orders from its training
endQuiz.explain: Scout touches the outside world only through tools. That keeps the data fresh and makes every access visible in the trace.
endQuiz.hint: Look at what sits between the loop and the data on the hub.

endQuiz.q: A customer asks Scout which climbing rope to buy. What does the design say Scout should do?
options: Hand the chat to a person with a short summary
Say it can't help and end the chat
endQuiz.explain: Product advice is outside Scout's job. A hand-off with a summary gets the customer to someone who can help, without making them repeat themselves.
endQuiz.hint: The architecture has a path built for exactly this.
